tldr.lead: Zoom, Google Meet and Microsoft Teams all show free live captions, but none of them lets a free account keep the text. A Chrome extension can, from the tab or the speakers your class plays through.

Google Meet: transcripts are saved to the organizer's Google Drive only on paid Workspace editions. Education Fundamentals, the free plan most schools use, does not include them.
Microsoft Teams: live captions are available to every user and are never saved. Transcription is an admin policy and is stored with the recording in OneDrive or SharePoint.

intro: The free way to transcribe a Zoom, Google Meet or Microsoft Teams class is to capture it in Chrome with an extension such as LessonScriptor, because the platforms' own free tiers show live captions but do not let you keep them. Zoom's saved transcripts start at the Pro plan, Google Meet transcripts need a paid Workspace edition, and Teams transcription depends on your school's admin policy. LessonScriptor builds an editable transcript in a side panel while the class runs, with no bot in the call and no account. This guide covers what each platform gives you for free, the difference between meeting bots and browser capture, which setup works for students and which for teachers, and how to share a transcript without breaking anyone's trust.

sections.h2: What is the free way to transcribe a Zoom, Google Meet or Teams class?
sections.body:
A free class transcript is a text copy of what was said that you can keep, search and edit after the call ends. Zoom, Google Meet and Microsoft Teams each offer live captions at no cost, but captions are a display feature: they scroll past on screen and vanish when the meeting closes. The saved version, the transcript file, sits behind a paid plan or an admin setting on all three.

That leaves two free routes. The first is to get whoever hosts the class to turn on the built-in transcript, if their plan has it. The second is to transcribe on your own computer: a Chrome extension such as LessonScriptor listens to the class as it plays and writes the transcript into a side panel you control. The second route works whatever plan the host is on, and it works for recordings too.

The rest of this guide goes platform by platform, because the details differ, and the difference between a student listening in and a teacher speaking changes which setup you need.

sections.h2: Does Zoom have free built-in transcription?
sections.body:
Zoom has free live captions, but its saved transcripts are a paid feature. Zoom offers three things that are easy to mix up, and only one of them is free.

**Live captions** work on every Zoom account, including free Basic accounts. Since Zoom split captions and transcripts in late May 2026, captions are live only: participants can scroll back about three minutes and cannot save or download them. The old "Save captions" button is gone.

**Meeting transcript** is the new saved transcript, separate from captions since that May 2026 change. It needs a Pro, Business or Enterprise account, it is off by default, and the host has to start it from the More menu in the Zoom desktop or mobile app. Participants can request access, and the host decides whether to approve. Saved transcripts land as a .txt file in the Zoom folder of your Documents.

**Audio transcript for cloud recordings** is a file Zoom generates after a cloud recording finishes. It needs a paid account with cloud recording, plus an owner or admin who has enabled audio transcription in the recording settings. It also takes time to process after the meeting.

The **Zoom chat transcript** is a fourth thing people find when they search: it saves typed messages, not speech. On a free account, or in a class where the host has not turned anything on, Zoom gives you no way to keep what was said.

sections.h2: Does Google Meet have free transcripts?
sections.body:
Google Meet transcripts are not free. The Transcripts feature saves a Google Doc to the meeting organizer's Drive after the call, with speaker names and timestamps. It is included in Business Standard, Business Plus, Enterprise Starter, Enterprise Standard and Enterprise Plus, Workspace Individual, Education Plus and the Teaching and Learning Upgrade.

It is not available in Education Fundamentals, the free edition most schools and universities run on, or in Education Standard, Business Starter, Essentials and personal Gmail accounts. Even where a school pays for it, accounts with a student licence have transcripts turned off by default. In practice, a student can almost never start a Meet transcript, and a teacher can only do so if the school has bought one of the right editions.

Google Meet's live captions, on the other hand, are free on all accounts. Like Zoom's, they are for reading during the call and are not saved as a document.

sections.h2: Does Microsoft Teams have live captions and transcription?
sections.body:
Microsoft Teams has both, but only captions are guaranteed. Live captions with speaker attribution are available to Teams users and can be turned on from the meeting menu. Microsoft is explicit that Teams does not save captions.

Transcription is a separate policy that the school or company admin controls. Both the organizer and the person who starts the transcript need it allowed in their meeting policy. The transcript is then stored with the meeting recording in OneDrive or SharePoint, where participants can view it after the meeting, with timestamps and speaker names. Translated captions and translated transcripts need a Teams Premium licence for the organizer.

Many universities that run Microsoft 365 leave transcription on, so it is worth checking with your IT service before installing anything. If the option is greyed out in your meeting, it is a policy decision, and the browser route below still works because Teams runs in Chrome at teams.microsoft.com.

sections.h2: Meeting bot or browser extension: what is the difference?
sections.body:
A meeting bot is a transcription service that joins your call as an extra participant. Otter.ai, Fireflies.ai and similar tools connect to your calendar, send a bot named something like "Otter Notetaker" into the Zoom, Meet or Teams call, and record from inside the meeting. Everyone sees it in the participant list, the host may have to admit it from the waiting room, and many universities block unknown bots outright.

Bots have real strengths. They label who said what, they can attend a meeting you are not in, and they produce summaries. For a team meeting with five speakers, that is often what you want, and LessonScriptor does not do speaker identification or summaries.

A browser extension works differently. LessonScriptor runs on your own computer and transcribes what your Chrome tab plays, or what your speakers play, so nothing joins the call and nobody else needs to install anything. That is why it works in classes where bots are blocked, on recorded lectures where there is no meeting to join, and without connecting your calendar or creating an account. The trade-off is that it only hears what reaches your computer, and you need to be there with Chrome open.

sections.h2: Which LessonScriptor mode works for my class setup?
sections.body:
LessonScriptor has two ways of listening, and the right one depends on whether you are listening to the class or teaching it.

**Free mode** uses Chrome's built-in speech recognition through your microphone. It is free forever, needs no account, and sends no audio to LessonScriptor's servers. Because it listens through the mic, it hears your own voice plus whatever comes out of your speakers. It does not work with headphones, and the volume should be around 80% or higher.

**AI mode** captures the audio of the Chrome tab directly and sends it in short chunks to a cloud speech model, so it works with headphones and handles accents and technical terms much better. Text appears every 10 seconds in Normal mode or every 30 seconds in Optimal mode. It is pay as you go: a 30-minute free trial, then one-time packs of 5 hours for $5, 15 hours for $12 or 30 hours for $21. Credits never expire, and Stripe shows the price in your local currency at checkout.

subsections.h3: Student watching a live class in the browser
subsections.body: Join through Google Meet in Chrome, Teams on the web, or Zoom's "Join from your browser" link. AI mode captures the tab, so headphones are fine and your own voice is not mixed in. Free mode also works if you use speakers.

Use Free mode with speakers, not headphones. The mic picks up your voice directly and the students' questions as your speakers play them. AI mode only captures what the tab plays, and a video call does not play your own voice back to you, so an AI mode transcript of your own class would be missing you.

subsections.h3: Zoom, Teams or Webex desktop app
subsections.body: AI mode cannot reach audio outside Chrome. Free mode still works, because the microphone hears the desktop app through your speakers. Keep the volume high and the room quiet. If you can, switch to the browser version of the meeting instead.

Open the recording in a Chrome tab and use AI mode for the cleanest result. You can play the recording at normal speed while you do something else in another tab, since each tab is captured on its own.

sections.h2: How do I transcribe a Zoom, Meet or Teams class in Chrome?
sections.body: The whole setup takes about two minutes the first time, and nothing changes for anyone else in the call.
steps: Install LessonScriptor from the Chrome Web Store. Free mode needs no sign-up.
Open the class in Chrome: Google Meet runs in the browser already, Teams works at teams.microsoft.com, and Zoom meetings have a "Join from your browser" link on the launch page.
Click the LessonScriptor icon to open the side panel and choose the language of the class.
Pick the mode for your setup: Free mode with speakers if you are teaching or using a desktop app, AI mode if you are listening in a browser tab with headphones.
Press Record before the class starts. The transcript builds in the panel as people speak.
Edit as you go or after the call: bold key terms, add a header for each topic, highlight in one of five colours, or take a screenshot of a slide into the transcript.
Export as .txt or .md, or copy to your clipboard. Sessions are also saved automatically in the extension's history.

sections.h2: Can I transcribe a Zoom recording instead of the live call?
sections.body:
Yes. A Zoom recording is just a video once it plays in Chrome, so LessonScriptor transcribes it the same way as a live class, with no recording settings needed on the host's side. Open the cloud recording link at zoom.us in a Chrome tab, or the recording embedded in Canvas, Moodle or Blackboard, and press play. If you downloaded the .mp4, you can drag it into a Chrome tab and play it there.

The same goes for lecture capture systems such as Panopto, Kaltura and Echo360, Microsoft Stream recordings of Teams meetings, and YouTube. This is often the better option for students: you can pause, rewind a confusing passage, and the AI mode transcript is cleaner than one captured through speakers in a noisy room.

sections.h2: How can teachers share a class transcript with students?
sections.body:
A class transcript is most useful when it is edited and posted the same day. The raw text is a courtesy; a tidied one is something students can study from. These edits take ten minutes in LessonScriptor's editor, and you can do most of them while the class is still running:

Cut the setup minutes before the first sentence of content. Add one header per part of the lesson, so absent students can jump to what they missed. Bold the homework, the test date and any term you spelled out loud. Delete the tangent about the projector. Keep your own phrasing, because that is what students remember hearing.

Then export and post it where students already look: paste it into Google Classroom, a Moodle or Canvas page, a Teams channel, or an email. Markdown export keeps your headers and bold. Students do not need to install anything to read it.

callout.label: Before you post a transcript
callout.body: **Remove** student names attached to personal questions. **Fix** proper nouns and subject terms the speech engine misheard. **Add** the date and course name at the top. **Tell** students it is machine-generated, so they check anything that looks off.

sections.h2: Do class transcripts help with accessibility?
sections.body:
Class transcripts help four groups most: students who are deaf or hard of hearing, students with ADHD or dyslexia, students taking the class in a second language, and students who missed the session. For a student with ADHD, a transcript removes the need to listen and write at the same time, which is where attention usually breaks. For a second-language student, reading along turns half-understood sentences into something they can look up.

An automatic transcript is a support, not a guarantee. Speech engines still mishear names and formulas, and they do not describe what was on the slides. Where a student has a formal accommodation for captioning or note-taking, the university's disability service decides what counts, and that may be a human captioner. Use the transcript alongside the accommodation, and add slide screenshots to it so the text and the visuals stay together.

sections.h2: Is it OK to transcribe a class or meeting without telling anyone?
sections.body:
No. Tell people before you transcribe. A meeting bot announces itself in the participant list, and Zoom, Meet and Teams show a banner when their own transcription starts. A browser extension shows nothing to the other participants, so the duty to inform them falls on you. Recording and transcription rules vary by country and by institution. Many universities have a policy on capturing lectures, and in many places recording a conversation requires the consent of everyone in it. A one-line message at the start of the call ("I'm transcribing this to share notes afterwards") covers most situations, and teachers should say where the transcript will be posted.

On the data side, Free mode runs on Chrome's speech recognition and sends no audio to LessonScriptor's servers. In AI mode, short audio chunks from the tab are sent to a cloud transcription provider (Groq's Whisper model), which does not retain them beyond the request, according to LessonScriptor's privacy policy. In both modes the transcript is stored in your browser, not on a LessonScriptor server. LessonScriptor never records or saves the audio or video itself, only the text.

questions.question: Can I transcribe a Zoom meeting for free?
questions.answer: Not with Zoom's own tools on a free account. Zoom's live captions are free but cannot be saved, and saved meeting transcripts need a Pro plan or higher. LessonScriptor's Free mode transcribes a Zoom meeting through your microphone and speakers at no cost and keeps an editable transcript.

questions.question: Can I get a Zoom transcript without recording the meeting?
questions.answer: Yes. Since May 2026, Zoom's meeting transcript no longer depends on a cloud recording, but it needs a Pro account or higher and the host has to start it. LessonScriptor needs no recording either: it transcribes the live audio as the meeting plays.

questions.question: Can I get a Google Meet transcript on a free account?
questions.answer: Not from Google. Meet transcripts need a paid Workspace edition such as Business Standard, Education Plus or the Teaching and Learning Upgrade, and they are not included in Education Fundamentals. LessonScriptor works on any Meet call running in Chrome, whatever the plan.

questions.question: Does LessonScriptor work with the Zoom or Teams desktop app?
questions.answer: Only in Free mode. Free mode listens through your microphone, so it hears the desktop app through your speakers. AI mode captures Chrome tab audio, so it needs the meeting open in the browser, for example through Zoom's "Join from your browser" link or Teams on the web.

questions.question: Does LessonScriptor join the call like Otter or Fireflies?
questions.answer: No. LessonScriptor has no meeting bot. It runs in your Chrome browser and transcribes what your tab or speakers play, so nothing appears in the participant list. Because of that, you should tell the other participants that you are transcribing.

questions.question: I teach on Google Meet. Which mode captures my own voice?
questions.answer: Free mode with speakers. It listens through your microphone, so it hears you directly and hears students through the speakers. AI mode captures only what the tab plays, and the call does not play your own voice back, so your part would be missing.

summary.heading: A transcript of every class, whatever plan the host is on
summary.body: Zoom, Google Meet and Teams give everyone free captions and keep the saved transcript for paid plans or admin settings. LessonScriptor closes that gap from your own Chrome browser: Free mode through the speakers for teachers and desktop apps, AI mode on the tab for students and recordings, no bot in the call, and an editable transcript you can share the same day.
